'''Abigail Gutmann Doyle''' is a professor of chemistry at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], where she holds the Saul Winstein Chair in Organic Chemistry.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Jennings|first=Penny|date=Jun 30, 2021|title=Welcome Professor Abigail Doyle {{!}} UCLA Chemistry and Biochemistry|url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/welcome-professor-abigail-doyle|access-date=2021-07-01|website=www.chemistry.ucla.edu}}</ref> Her research often covers the development of new chemical transformations in organic chemistry.

== Early life and education ==
Doyle was born in Princeton, NJ in 1980 to [[Michael W. Doyle]] and [[Amy Gutmann]], the eighth [[List of presidents of University of Pennsylvania|president]] of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and later the [[United States Ambassador to Germany]]. Doyle studied Chemistry and Chemical Biology as an undergraduate at [[Harvard University]], graduating with A.B. and A.M. degrees ''[[summa cum laude]]'' in 2002.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Abigail G. Doyle, Princeton University {{!}} Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.stanford.edu/events/professor-abigail-g-doyle-princeton-university |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=chemistry.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref> Here, she met her husband Jakub Jurek.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2005-06-26 |title=Abigail Doyle and Jakub Jurek |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/26/fashion/weddings/abigail-doyle-and-jakub-jurek.html |access-date=2026-03-02 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In 2003, she went to Harvard University and joined the lab of Professor Eric Jacobsen.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Acceleration Consortium |url=https://acceleration.utoronto.ca/researcher/abigail-doyle |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=acceleration.utoronto.ca}}</ref> Here her work included the research on a transition metal-catalyzed enatioselective.<ref>{{Cite web |last=jamie |title=Abby |url=https://doyle.chem.ucla.edu/abby/ |access-date=2026-10-05 |website=The Doyle Group |language=en-US}}</ref>

After beginning graduate studies in the lab of Justin DuBois at [[Stanford University]] as a pre-doctoral fellow, Doyle completed her Ph.D. under Prof. [[Eric Jacobsen (chemist)|Eric N. Jacobsen]] at Harvard, where she collaborated with Dr. Christina White<ref>{{Cite web |last=jamie |title=Abby |url=https://doyle.chem.ucla.edu/abby/ |access-date=2026-10-08 |website=The Doyle Group |language=en-US}}</ref> in developing [[Enantioselective synthesis|enantioselective]] alkylations with [[Enolate|tributyltin enolates]] catalyzed by a [[Metal salen complexes|Cr(salen)Cl catalyst]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Doyle|first1=Abigail G.|last2=Jacobsen|first2=Eric N.|date=2005-01-01|title=Enantioselective Alkylations of Tributyltin Enolates Catalyzed by Cr(salen)Cl: Access to Enantiomerically Enriched All-Carbon Quaternary Centers|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=127|issue=1|pages=62–63|doi=10.1021/ja043601p|pmid=15631449|bibcode=2005JAChS.127...62D |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Doyle|first1=Abigail G.|last2=Jacobsen|first2=Eric N.|date=2007|title=Enantioselective Alkylation of Acyclic α,α-Disubstituted Tributyltin Enolates Catalyzed by a Cr(salen) Complex|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/anie.200604901|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|volume=46|issue=20|pages=3701–3705|doi=10.1002/anie.200604901|pmid=17407117|issn=1521-3773|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=アビー・ドイル Abigail G. Doyle {{!}} Chem-Station (ケムステ) |url=https://www.chem-station.com/chemist-db/2017/06/abigail-g-doyle.html |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=www.chem-station.com |language=ja}}</ref> She also worked on the development of an [[Enantioselective synthesis|enantioselective]] addition of nucleophiles to [[Oxocarbenium|oxocarbenium ions]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Reisman|first1=Sarah E.|last2=Doyle|first2=Abigail G.|last3=Jacobsen|first3=Eric N.|date=2008-06-01|title=Enantioselective Thiourea-Catalyzed Additions to Oxocarbenium Ions|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=130|issue=23|pages=7198–7199|doi=10.1021/ja801514m|issn=0002-7863|pmc=2574628|pmid=18479086|bibcode=2008JAChS.130.7198R }}</ref> Here, she was a recipient of a National Science Foundation fellowship.<ref name=":0" /> At the end of her studies at Harvard she received her AB and AM summa cum laude in chemistry and chemical biology.<ref name=":1" />

== Career ==

;Independent career

In July 2008, Doyle was appointed as an assistant professor of chemistry at Princeton University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chemistry's new 'cathedral' a beacon to young faculty {{!}} Princeton Alumni Weekly |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/article/chemistrys-new-cathedral-beacon-young-faculty |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=paw.princeton.edu |language=en}}</ref> She was promoted to the rank of associate professor with tenure in 2013, and to full Professor with an endowed chair, the A. Barton Hepburn Professor of Chemistry, in 2017.<ref name="chemlabs.princeton.edu">[http://chemlabs.princeton.edu/doyle/people/about-abby/ The Doyle Group] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114155615/http://chemlabs.princeton.edu/doyle/people/about-abby/|date=2017-11-14}}, Princeton University</ref> In 2021, she moved to the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], where she holds the Saul Winstein Chair in Organic Chemistry. She studies catalysis and physical organic chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Doyle, Abigail – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241111125823/https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |archive-date=2024-11-11 |access-date=2025-02-10 |website=www.chemistry.ucla.edu |language=en-US |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Doyle specializes in organic, inorganic, and Theory and Computation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Doyle, Abigail – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |access-date=2026-10-26 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Doyle advised 2026 Sloan Research Fellow, Erin Stache.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 17, 2026 |title=Seven faculty members win Sloan Research Fellowships for early-career researchers |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2026/02/17/seven-faculty-members-win-sloan-research-fellowships-early-career-researchers |access-date=2026-02-21 |website=Princeton University |language=en}}</ref> 

In 2021 She was selected as one of the Cell Press 50 scientists.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cell Press - Search Results: Cell Press|url=https://www.cell.com/topic/cell-do-taxonomy/cell-news-inspiring-scientists|website=www.cell.com|access-date=2026-02-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126223945/https://www.cell.com/topic/cell-do-taxonomy/cell-news-inspiring-scientists|archive-date=2024-11-26|language=en}}</ref>

When transitioning from her traditional lab organic chemistry toward machine learning, Abigail Doyle stated that her biggest obstacle wasn't the technology itself, but a literal data science language barrier. In a video interview, she highlighted how difficult it was for physical organic chemists and computer scientists to collaborate due to the lack of a shared vocabulary to describe chemical behaviors and coding parameters.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FJs6Q5veNTI |title=Zoomin' with Abby Doyle - The proof is in the pudding |date=2020-07-15 |last=Center for Computer-Assisted Synthesis |access-date=2026-09-29 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

'''Research'''

Her lab, the Doyle Lab Group, specializes in organic, computational, and physical organic chemistry. One of the group's main priority is to solve problems that the field has with organic synthesis by creating catalytic reactions and synthetic processes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Acceleration Consortium |url=https://acceleration.utoronto.ca/researcher/abigail-doyle |access-date=2025-09-07 |website=acceleration.utoronto.ca}}</ref> A longstanding research interest of the Doyle group is the development of nickel-catalyzed C–C bond forming reactions that utilize unconventional cross-coupling electrophiles, such as epoxides, aziridines, imminium ions, and oxocarbenium ions<ref>{{Cite web |last=jamie |title=Ni Cross-Coupling |url=https://doyle.chem.ucla.edu/ni-catalyzed-cross-coupling/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=The Doyle Group |language=en-US}}</ref>. The group has developed and mechanistically interrogated new ligands and pre-catalysts for nickel, which have helped to enable these transformations. In collaboration with [[David MacMillan]]'s group, the Doyle lab identified a new cross-coupling paradigm which allows the combination of photoredox and nickel catalysis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zuo|first1=Zhiwei|last2=Ahneman|first2=Derek T.|last3=Chu|first3=Lingling|last4=Terrett|first4=Jack A.|last5=Doyle|first5=Abigail G.|last6=MacMillan|first6=David W. C.|date=2014-07-25|title=Merging photoredox with nickel catalysis: Coupling of α-carboxyl sp3-carbons with aryl halides|journal=Science|language=en|volume=345|issue=6195|pages=437–440|doi=10.1126/science.1255525|issn=0036-8075|pmc=4296524|pmid=24903563|bibcode=2014Sci...345..437Z}}</ref> One nickel pre-catalyst that was developed by Doyle and Monfette was suitable for rapid screening and could be used in various types of cataytic reactions. This includes Buchwald coupling and Suzuki-Miyaura.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=John |first=Morgan E. |last2=Koutsantonis |first2=George A. |last3=Dorta |first3=Reto |last4=Stewart |first4=Scott G. |title=Well-Defined Nickel Precatalysts: Form, Function, and Application |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/chem.71481 |journal=Chemistry – A European Journal |language=en |volume=n/a |issue=n/a |pages=e71481 |doi=10.1002/chem.71481 |issn=1521-3765}}</ref> The Doyle lab has subsequently applied Nickel/photoredox catalysis to methodologies involving both unconventional and traditional cross-coupling electrophiles.

The group has also been involved in the development of nucleophilic fluorination chemistry allowing the creation of pharmaceutically relevant molecules with sp<sup>3</sup>-C-F and sp<sup>2</sup>-C-F bonds. There is limitations to the production of fluorinated compounds due to the lack of availability of synthetic materials needed to produce C-F bonds<ref>{{Cite web |title=Abigail Doyle {{!}} NSF BioPACIFIC MIP (DMR-2445868) |url=https://biopacificmip.org/people/faculty/abigail-doyle |access-date=2026-09-19 |website=biopacificmip.org}}</ref>. These methods have employed both transition metal and photoredox catalysis, and the group has developed new reagents for mild and selective deoxyfluorination reactions. 

Recently, the Doyle group has worked in the area of data science-driven analysis of chemical reactions, including the implementation of machine learning algorithms to model and predict reaction outcome in organic chemistry.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ahneman|first1=Derek T.|last2=Estrada|first2=Jesus G. J.|last3=Lin|first3=Shishi|last4=Dreher|first4=Spencer D.|last5=Doyle|first5=Abigail G.|date=2018-02-15|title=Predicting reaction performance in C–N cross-coupling using machine learning|journal=Science|language=en|volume=360|issue=6385|pages=186–190|doi= 10.1126/science.aar5169|pmid=29449509 |bibcode=2018Sci...360..186A |s2cid=206666015 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shields|first1=Benjamin J.|last2=Stevens|first2=Jason|last3=Li|first3=Jun|last4=Parasram|first4=Marvin|last5=Damani|first5=Farhan|last6=Martinez Alvarado|first6=Jesus I.|last7=Janey|first7=Jacob M.|last8=Adams|first8=Ryan P.|last9=Doyle|first9=Abigail G.|date=2021-02-03|title=Bayyesian reaction optimization as a tool for chemical synthesis|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=590|issue=7844 |pages=89–96|doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03213-y|pmid= 33536653|bibcode=2021Natur.590...89S |s2cid=231804657 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Żurański|first1=Andrzej M.|last2=Martinez Alvarado|first2=Jesus I.|last3=Shields|first3=Benjamin J.|last4=Doyle|first4=Abigail G.|date=2021-03-31|title=Predicting Reaction Yields via Supervised Learning|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|language=en|volume=54|issue=8 |pages=1856–1865|doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00770|pmid=33788552 |s2cid=232483029 }}</ref> Her most recent publication is on the "Markovnikov hydroamination of terminal alkenes via phosphine redox catalysis," published in the Nature journal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fan |first=Flora |last2=Sedillo |first2=Kassandra F. |last3=Maertens |first3=Alexander J. |last4=Doyle |first4=Abigail G. |date=2026-02-23 |title=Markovnikov hydroamination of terminal alkenes via phosphine redox catalysis |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10263-7 |journal=Nature |language=en |pages=1–2 |doi=10.1038/s41586-026-10263-7 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref> Doyle's lab has also been utilizing these computer-assisted techniques as an aid to improve the design of their catalysts as well as the exploration of new reactions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Doyle, Abigail – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250524215210/https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |archive-date=2025-05-24 |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=www.chemistry.ucla.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>

Early on in 2026, Doyle had the opportunity to co-lead a research team alongside her research partner [[Matthew Sigman|Mathew S. Sigman]]. Together they were able to create a prediction system which used learned based functions to help accelerate the processes of drug discovery. This study focused on the predictions of nickel-catalyzed reaction outcomes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Potter |first=Lisa |date=March 12, 2026 |title=AI tool predicts drug-building reactions, speeding discovery |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/ai-tool-predicts-drug-building-reactions-speeding-discovery/#:~:text=A%20research%20team%20co%2Dled,together%20with%20Professor%20Matthew%20S.&text=%E2%80%9COne%20of%20the%20nice%20things,have%20learned%20without%20the%20tool.%E2%80%9D |url-status=live |access-date=April 12, 2026 |website=University of California Chemistry and Biochemistry}}</ref>
== Awards and honors ==
Some key awards of Doyle's independent career include the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation Fellowship ([[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], 2012),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sloan.org/past-fellows|title=Past Fellows|website=sloan.org|access-date=2018-09-02|archive-date=2018-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows}}</ref> Amgen Young Investigator Award (2012), [[Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award]] ([[American Chemical Society]], 2014), sponsored by ASC Corporation Associates (recipients are awarded at the fall ASC national meeting),<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2015-01-26 |title=ACS National Award Winners |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/cen-09304-awards1 |journal=Chemical & Engineering News Archive |language=en |volume=93 |issue=4 |pages=40–43 |doi=10.1021/cen-09304-awards1 |issn=0009-2347|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/92/i11/2014-Arthur-C-Cope-Scholar0.html|title=2014 Arthur C. Cope Scholar Awards: Abigail G. Doyle {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Ritter|first=Stephen K.|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2018-09-02}}</ref>  Bayer Early Excellence in Science Award (2013), [[Phi Lambda Upsilon]] National Fresenius Award (Phi Lamba Upsilon, 2014), Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE, 2014) BMS Unrestricted Grant in Synthetic Organic Chemistry (2016).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Abigail Doyle {{!}} Princeton University Department of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/abigail-doyle#honors|access-date=2020-10-27|website=chemistry.princeton.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024174608/https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/abigail-doyle#honors|archive-date=2020-10-24|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2012, Doyle received the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers. She was given this award for her contributions to medicinal chemistry and chemical biology, as well as her contributions in mentoring elementary scientists.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Abigail Doyle {{!}} NSF - U.S. National Science Foundation |url=https://www.nsf.gov/honorary-awards/pecase/recipients/abigail-doyle |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.nsf.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In 2019 she received the RSC Fluorine Award and the 15th Hirata Prize.<ref name=":2" />

In 2020 she became an [[American Chemical Society]] Fellow.<ref name=":2" />

In 2021, Doyle became a chair of Organic Chemistry at the University of California, Los Angeles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=jamie |title=Abby |url=https://doyle.chem.ucla.edu/abby/ |access-date=2025-10-31 |website=The Doyle Group |language=en-US}}</ref> She also won the Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation Machine Learning in the Chemical Sciences and Engineering Award. 

In 2022, she won the EJ Corey Award for Outstanding Original Contribution in Organic Synthesis by a Young Investigator. 

She was a finalist for the [[Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists|Blavatnik National Award for Young Scientists]] in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024 |title=US National Honorees |url=https://blavatnikawards.org/honorees/national-finalists/ |website=Blavatnik Awards}}</ref>

She is currently senior editor of ''[[Accounts of Chemical Research]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/achre4/editors.html|title=Editors|website=pubs.acs.org|language=en|access-date=2018-09-02}}</ref>

In 2023, Doyle was awarded the OMCOS award for her major contributions to organometallic chemistry and organic synthesis.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lau |first=Will |title=2023 OMCOS Award for Abby |url=https://doyle.chem.ucla.edu/2023-omcos-award-for-abby/ |access-date=2025-10-28 |website=The Doyle Group |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2024, Doyle became a MAVEN senior scientist, an award that will present her work and serve as inspiration to newly tenured women scientists.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 23, 2026 |title=Doyle, Abigail - UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/directory/doyle-abigail/ |url-status=live |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=Ucla.edu}}</ref> Doyle also received the Ta-Shue Chou Lectureship Award in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ta-shue Chou Lectureship |url=https://tschou.chem.sinica.edu.tw/conf.php?m=awards |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=tschou.chem.sinica.edu.tw}}</ref> She was given this award to recognize her outstanding work in organic chemistry as a mid-career scientist.

In 2026, Doyle and her collaborators were awarded $19.5 million to establish an open-access autonomous chemistry laboratory.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2026-08-26 |title=Abigail Doyle and collaborators awarded $19.5 million to establish an open-access autonomous chemistry laboratory – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/abigail-doyle-and-collaborators-awarded-19-5-million-to-establish-an-open-access-autonomous-chemistry-laboratory/ |access-date=2026-09-10 |language=en-US}}</ref> She is set to expand data-rich experimental design and research new catalytic reactions.<ref name=":3" />

In 2026, Doyle received UCLA's 2026-27 Excellence in Postdoctoral Mentoring Award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-10-22 |title=Abigail Doyle receives 2026–27 Excellence in Postdoctoral Mentoring Award – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/abigail-doyle-receives-2026-27-excellence-in-postdoctoral-mentoring-award/ |access-date=2026-10-27 |language=en-US}}</ref> 

In 2026, Doyle and collaborators at Scripps Research Institute and Sunthetics received the National Science Foundation Award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-10-22 |title=Abigail Doyle receives 2026–27 Excellence in Postdoctoral Mentoring Award – UCLA |url=https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/abigail-doyle-receives-2026-27-excellence-in-postdoctoral-mentoring-award/ |access-date=2026-10-27 |language=en-US}}</ref>
